title: APIs & Networking
description: How clients and servers talk to each other over the network.

lessons.title: What happens during an API request?

blocks.text: A server is a program that waits for requests and answers them. The client, such as a browser or a phone, is the one that asks.

steps: Client sends a request
Server checks who is asking
Server runs the logic
Server reads or writes data
Server sends a response

blocks.text: Each request stands on its own. The server knows who is asking only if the request says so, usually with a token that proves the login.

blocks.code:
api/
├── controllers/    receive requests, return responses
├── services/       the rules of the app
├── repositories/   talk to the database
└── models/         the shape of the data

items: Expecting the server to remember the previous request without a token or session.
Putting business rules in controllers, so the same rule ends up copied in many places.
Treating a request as instant and forgetting that the network can be slow or fail.

blocks.text: A request travels through layers in order, and each layer does one job. Every request has to carry everything the server needs to answer it.

lessons.title: HTTP methods: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE

blocks.text: A method tells the server what the client wants to do. The same address can accept different methods, and each one means something different.

blocks.code:
GET     /lessons/12    read lesson 12
DELETE  /lessons/12    remove lesson 12
POST    /lessons       create a new lesson

items: Changing data in a GET request, so a page refresh or a link preview changes things.
Retrying a failed POST automatically and creating the same item twice.
Using POST for everything, which hides what each request actually does.

blocks.text: Repeating a GET is safe because it changes nothing. Repeating a POST may create a second item, so pick the method that matches the intent.
Every response starts with a three-digit status code. The first digit tells the client what kind of answer it got before it reads anything else.
The range decides what the client should do next. A 4xx means fix the request; a 5xx means the same request may work later.

items: Returning 200 with an error message in the body, so clients and monitoring think everything worked.
Using 500 for invalid input, which blames the server for the client’s mistake.
Retrying 4xx responses that will fail the same way every time.

blocks.text: The status code is the first and most important part of the answer. Pick the one that tells the client what to do next.
Headers are key-value pairs that travel with a request or a response. They carry information about the message rather than the message itself.

blocks.code:
GET /api/lessons/12
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...   who is asking
Accept: application/json             what format the client wants

200 OK
Content-Type: application/json       what format the body is in
Cache-Control: max-age=60            how long it may be reused

items: Sending JSON without a Content-Type header, so the server cannot parse it.
Putting secrets in custom headers that end up in logs.

blocks.text: The body is the content; headers are the instructions for handling it.
REST organizes an API around resources: things with an address, such as a lesson or a user. The method says what to do with the resource.

blocks.code:
GET     /lessons          list lessons
POST    /lessons          create a lesson
GET     /lessons/12       read lesson 12
PATCH   /lessons/12       change part of lesson 12
DELETE  /lessons/12       remove lesson 12
GET     /lessons/12/quiz  a resource that belongs to lesson 12

items: Putting verbs in the address, such as /getLesson or /deleteLesson, instead of using the method.
Returning a different shape for the same resource from different endpoints.

blocks.text: Addresses name things, methods name actions. Keep both predictable and clients can guess the rest.
The network is slow or broken more often than it seems. A request without a timeout can wait forever and hold resources the whole time.

steps: Send the request with a timeout
No answer in time: stop waiting
Wait a little, then retry
Wait longer before each next retry
Give up after a few tries and show an error

items: Calling other services without a timeout.
Retrying immediately and in a tight loop, which overloads a server that is already struggling.
Retrying requests that are not safe to repeat, such as a payment.

blocks.text: Every network call needs a timeout. Retry with growing pauses, and only when repeating is safe.
A rate limit caps how many requests a client may send in a time window. It protects the server from overload and from abuse such as password guessing.

blocks.code:
POST /api/auth/login

429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 30
{ "title": "Too many login attempts. Try again in 30 seconds." }

items: Limiting only by IP address, so many users behind one network block each other.
Not telling the client when it may try again.

blocks.text: Answer with 429 and Retry-After, and let clients slow down instead of failing blindly.
HTTP can tell browsers and proxies how long a response stays fresh. A fresh response is reused without asking the server again.

blocks.code:
200 OK
Cache-Control: max-age=300
ETag: "v42"

GET /api/categories
If-None-Match: "v42"
304 Not Modified          nothing changed, reuse the copy

items: Caching responses that contain one user’s private data in a shared cache.
Setting a long max-age on data that changes often, so users see stale results.

blocks.text: Cache-Control decides how long a copy is fresh; ETag lets the client ask cheaply whether it changed.

lessons.title: CORS: why the browser blocks a request

blocks.text: Browsers block a page from reading responses from another origin unless that server allows it. CORS is how the server says which origins are allowed.

steps: app.devbrawl.io calls api.devbrawl.io
The browser sends a preflight OPTIONS request
The API answers with Access-Control-Allow-Origin
The browser checks the origin is allowed
Only then the real request goes out

items: Allowing every origin with * on an API that uses cookies.
Trying to fix CORS in the frontend; only the server can allow an origin.

blocks.text: CORS is enforced by the browser and configured on the server. Allow exactly the origins you trust.
Some data changes while the user watches, such as a duel score. The client can ask again and again, or keep one connection open and let the server push.

rows: The client asks every few seconds
The server holds the request until there is news
One open connection, messages both ways

items: Polling every second for data that changes once an hour.
Forgetting to reconnect when a WebSocket drops.

blocks.text: Poll when updates are rare; keep a connection open when both sides need to talk in real time.

title: Databases
description: How data is stored, linked and kept consistent.

blocks.text: Data has to outlive a single request. A database keeps it safely and lets many users read and write at the same time.
A row is one record, and a column is one property that every record has. Because each column holds one kind of value, the data stays predictable.

steps: Create a record
Read records that match
Update a record
Delete a record

items: Storing several values in one column, such as a comma-separated list of tags.
Using a text column for numbers or dates, so sorting and comparing break.

blocks.text: Tables give every record the same shape. Create, read, update and delete cover most of the work a database does.
Copying the same data into many places causes mistakes. A better way is to store each fact once and link to it by a key.
The primary key identifies one row. A foreign key stores the primary key of a row in another table, such as winner_id pointing at users.id.

items: Copying the nickname into every duel, so a rename leaves old duels out of date.
Skipping the foreign key constraint, so a duel can point at a user that was deleted.
Using a value that can change, such as an email, as the primary key.

blocks.text: Store each fact once and link to it by key. The database can then guarantee that every link points at a real row.
Data that belongs together often lives in different tables. A join combines rows from two tables where a key matches, so one query can answer one question.

blocks.code:
SELECT duels.id, users.nickname AS winner
FROM duels
JOIN users ON users.id = duels.winner_id

rows: Only rows that match in both tables
Every row from the left table, matched or not

items: Forgetting the ON condition, which pairs every row with every other row.
Using an inner join when rows without a match must still show up.

blocks.text: Joins rebuild the full picture from tables that each store one kind of thing.
Without an index, the database reads every row to find a match. An index is a sorted lookup structure that jumps straight to the right rows.

blocks.code: CREATE INDEX ix_users_email ON users (email);

items: Indexing every column, which slows down every insert and update.
Adding an index but filtering with a function on the column, so the index is not used.

blocks.text: Index the columns you search and join on. Each index speeds up reads and costs a little on writes.
A transaction groups several changes so they happen together or not at all. ACID names the guarantees a transaction gives.

rows: All changes apply, or none do
Rules such as keys and constraints still hold afterwards
Running transactions do not see each other’s half-done work
Once committed, the change survives a crash

items: Running related updates as separate statements, so a crash in between leaves half a change.
Keeping a transaction open while waiting for a user or a network call.

blocks.text: Wrap changes that must stay together in one short transaction.
Normalization removes repeated data by splitting it into tables that each describe one thing. Each fact then lives in exactly one place.

blocks.code:
before:  duels(id, winner_nickname, winner_email, loser_nickname, ...)

after:   users(id, nickname, email)
         duels(id, winner_id → users.id, loser_id → users.id)

items: Copying user details into every row that mentions the user.
Splitting tables so far that every simple read needs many joins.

blocks.text: Store each fact once and link to it. Denormalize later only where a measured read needs it.
Loading a list and then one extra query per item turns one request into hundreds of database round trips. It is easy to write and slow to run.

blocks.file: one query for the list, N for the details
blocks.code:
duels = db.query("SELECT * FROM duels LIMIT 50")      1 query
for duel in duels:
    duel.winner = db.query("SELECT * FROM users",       50 queries
                           where id = duel.winner_id)

blocks.text: The fix loads the related rows in one go: a join, or one query with WHERE id IN (...) for all the ids.

items: Not noticing because it is fast with ten rows in development.
Lazy-loading relations inside a loop in an ORM.

blocks.text: Count queries per request. Load related data in bulk, not one row at a time.
Opening a database connection is slow. A pool keeps a few connections open and lends them to requests, which give them back when done.

steps: A request needs the database
It borrows a free connection from the pool
It runs its queries
It returns the connection
If none are free, the request waits for one

items: Forgetting to return a connection, so the pool slowly runs dry.
Making the pool bigger than the database can handle.

blocks.text: Borrow late, return early. A leaking pool looks like the database suddenly hanging.
The database structure changes as the app grows. Migrations are small, ordered scripts that move every database from one version to the next in the same way.

blocks.code:
Data/Migrations/
├── 20261024143436_AddAuth.cs
├── 20261024154840_AddCategories.cs
└── 20261024163755_AddDuels.cs

items: Changing the production schema by hand, so it no longer matches the migrations.
Editing a migration that already ran somewhere instead of adding a new one.

blocks.text: Every schema change is a new migration, applied in order, the same way everywhere.
Relational databases store rows in tables with a fixed shape. Document databases store whole objects, such as JSON, that can differ from each other.

rows: Embedded or looked up by id
Connected data that must stay consistent
Self-contained records read as a whole

items: Choosing a document store for highly connected data, then rebuilding joins in code.
Assuming “schemaless” means the data has no shape to maintain.

blocks.text: Pick the model that matches how the data is connected and read.

title: Security
description: How apps protect users, data and access.

blocks.text: Authentication answers who you are. Authorization answers what you are allowed to do. They are separate checks, and each one fails in its own way.

rows: Are you allowed to do this?

blocks.file: two requests to the same address
blocks.code:
GET /admin/users     no token
→ 401 Unauthorized   log in first

GET /admin/users     token of a regular user
→ 403 Forbidden      logged in, but not allowed

items: Returning 403 when the user is simply not logged in.
Checking permissions only in the frontend, where anyone can skip the check.
Trusting a user id sent in the request body instead of the one in the token.

blocks.text: Authentication proves identity, and authorization decides access. Check both on the server, on every request.
A server should never be able to read a password. Instead it stores a hash: the result of a one-way function that cannot be turned back into the password.

steps: The user picks a password
The server adds a random salt
The server runs a slow hash function
Only the salt and the hash are stored
At login, the same steps run and the results are compared

blocks.code:
id  email            password_hash
1   mara@mail.com    $2b$12$Kq8f...   salt + hash, never the password

items: Using a fast hash such as MD5 or SHA-1, which attackers can try billions of times per second.
Encrypting passwords instead of hashing them, so anyone with the key can read them.
Using the same salt for every user.

blocks.text: Store a slow, salted hash. If the database leaks, the passwords stay hard to recover.
When user input is glued into a SQL string, the input can change the query itself. An attacker can then read or delete data they should never reach.

blocks.file: the same search, unsafe and safe
blocks.code:
unsafe:  "SELECT * FROM users WHERE nickname = '" + input + "'"
         input = x' OR '1'='1   → returns every user

safe:    "SELECT * FROM users WHERE nickname = @nickname"
         the input is sent as a value, never as SQL

items: Escaping quotes by hand instead of using parameters.
Trusting input because it comes from your own frontend.

blocks.text: Always pass user input as query parameters. Never build SQL out of strings.
XSS happens when a page shows user content as HTML, so a script hidden in it runs in other users’ browsers with their session.

blocks.code: comment = unsafe: element.innerHTML = comment the script runs safe: element.textContent = comment shown as plain text

items: Rendering user content with innerHTML or dangerouslySetInnerHTML.
Sanitizing on input only, then reusing the data somewhere it is not escaped.

blocks.text: Treat user content as text. Escape it where it is shown, every time.
Browsers send cookies automatically. A malicious site can make your browser send a request to an app you are logged in to, and the cookie makes it look like you.

steps: You are logged in to bank.example
You open a malicious page
It submits a hidden form to bank.example/transfer
The browser adds your session cookie
Without protection, the bank accepts it

items: Changing data on GET requests, which any image tag can trigger.
Relying on cookies without SameSite or a CSRF token.

blocks.text: Use SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens or bearer tokens in headers, which other sites cannot add.
A JWT is a signed note from the server: “this is user 42 until 14:30”. The server can check the signature without looking anything up.

blocks.file: the three parts of a token
blocks.code:
header.payload.signature

header:     { "alg": "HS256" }
payload:    { "sub": "42", "exp": 1792860000 }   readable by anyone
signature:  proves the server issued it unchanged

items: Putting secrets in the payload, which is only encoded, not encrypted.
Issuing tokens that never expire.

blocks.text: A JWT proves who issued it and that it was not changed. Keep it short-lived and keep secrets out of it.
Plain HTTP travels as readable text, so anyone on the network can read or change it. HTTPS wraps it in TLS, which encrypts it and proves the server is who it claims to be.

steps: The browser connects to devbrawl.io
The server shows its certificate
The browser checks it was issued for that domain
Both agree on keys for this session
Everything after that is encrypted

items: Serving the login page over HTTPS but the API over plain HTTP.
Telling users to click through certificate warnings.

blocks.text: Use HTTPS everywhere. It protects both the content and the identity of the server.
Every user, service and key should have only the access it needs. When one of them is compromised, the damage stays small.

items: Letting the app connect to the database as a superuser.
Sharing one admin key between all services.

blocks.text: Grant the smallest access that works, and give each part its own credentials.
Repositories get copied, shared and published. A key committed once stays in the history even after the line is deleted.

blocks.code:
.gitignore        .env          never committed
.env              JWT_SECRET=...
.env.example      JWT_SECRET=   committed, without values

items: Committing a key and “fixing” it by deleting the line.
Printing configuration, secrets included, into build logs.

blocks.text: Load secrets from the environment. If one was ever committed, rotate it.
Frontend checks help users, but anyone can send a request without the frontend. The server must check every value it receives.

blocks.code:
nickname   3 to 20 letters, numbers or underscores
email      a valid address, not already used
password   at least 8 characters

anything else → 400 Bad Request with the reason

items: Validating only in the browser.
Accepting extra fields and saving them, such as "isAdmin": true.

blocks.text: Check type, size and allowed values on the server, and accept only the fields you expect.

title: Debugging
description: How to find out why code does not do what you expect.

blocks.text: When a program crashes, it prints the chain of calls that led to the crash. That chain is the stack trace, and it is the fastest map to the problem.

blocks.code:
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name')
    at formatWinner    (duel/result.ts:14)
    at showResult      (duel/screen.ts:42)
    at onDuelFinished  (duel/socket.ts:88)

steps: Read the message: what went wrong
Read the first line: where it broke
Read the lines below: who called it
Find where the bad value came from

items: Reading only the error message and skipping the location.
Assuming the fix always goes on the top line, when the caller passed the bad data.
Giving up when the top lines point into a library, while your own code is a few lines further down.

blocks.text: The message says what, the first line says where, and the lines below say how the program got there.
A bug you cannot trigger on purpose is a bug you cannot prove you fixed. The first job is to make it happen again, every time.

blocks.code:
Steps:     open a duel, answer the last question in under 1 second
Expected:  the result screen shows the winner
Actual:    the result screen is empty
Happens:   3 out of 3 tries

items.title: Reproduce
items.detail: Follow the steps until the bug appears on your machine.

items.title: Shrink
items.detail: Remove steps until only the ones that matter are left.

items.title: Find the cause
items.detail: Change one thing at a time and watch what changes.

items.title: Fix and confirm
items.detail: Run the same steps again and check the bug is gone.

items: Changing code before the bug can be reproduced.
Changing several things at once, so you cannot tell which one helped.
Testing only the usual path after the fix.

blocks.text: Make the bug happen on purpose, change one thing at a time, and confirm the fix with the same steps.
Logs are the app’s diary. Each line says when something happened, how serious it was, which part of the system wrote it and what happened.

blocks.code:
10:42:11 INFO  auth     POST /api/login 200
10:42:14 INFO  api      GET /api/profile 401
10:42:14 WARN  auth     Authorization header missing

blocks.text: The 401 is the symptom. The warning right after it is the cause: the request arrived without a token.

items: Searching only for ERROR lines, when the cause is often a WARN just before.
Logging without timestamps or request ids, so lines can’t be connected.

blocks.text: Read logs in time order around the failure, and separate symptoms from causes.
When something worked last week and is broken today, you don’t have to read every change. Test the middle commit and halve the search each time.

items.title: 64 commits to check
items.detail: The last good version and the first bad one are known.

items.title: Test commit 32
items.detail: Broken: the bug came in the first half.

items.title: Test commit 16
items.detail: Works: the bug is between 16 and 32.

items.title: About 6 steps later
items.detail: One commit is left. That is the one that broke it.

items: Reading the changes one by one from the newest backwards.
Testing with a flaky check, which sends the search the wrong way.

blocks.text: Halving the search finds one bad commit in 1 000 in about 10 tests. git bisect does it for you.
A debugger pauses the program on a chosen line, so you can see the real values instead of guessing them.

steps: Set a breakpoint just before the code that misbehaves
Run until it pauses there
Inspect the variables
Step one line at a time
Stop at the first value that differs from what you expect

items: Stepping through everything from the start instead of pausing near the problem.
Adding print statements and forgetting to remove them.

blocks.text: Pause where the problem starts and compare each value with what you expected.
Counting from 0 or 1, and stopping at < or <=, are easy to mix up. The result is a loop that skips the first item or reads one past the last.

blocks.code:
for (let i = 0; i <= rounds.length; i++)   reads rounds[5], which does not exist
for (let i = 0; i < rounds.length; i++)    reads rounds[0] to rounds[4]

items: Mixing 1-based line numbers with 0-based array indexes.
Testing only with lists of one item, where the bug hides.

blocks.text: Check the first and last item of every loop and every range.
A value that is missing where the code expects one causes some of the most common crashes. The crash happens where the value is used, not where it went missing.

blocks.code:
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'nickname')

const winner = players.find((p) => p.id === winnerId)   undefined if not found
show(winner.nickname)                                   crashes here

items: Fixing the crash line with a ?. without asking why the value was missing.
Assuming an API always returns every field.

blocks.text: Find where the value should have been set. Handle “not found” where it can happen.
When two operations run at the same time, the result can depend on which finishes first. The bug appears only sometimes, which makes it hard to catch.

items.title: Request A reads the score: 3
items.detail: Both requests start at the same moment.

items.title: Request B reads the score: 3
items.detail: B has not seen A’s change yet.

items.title: B writes 4
items.detail: B also adds one point to 3. One point is lost.

items: Reading a value, changing it in code and writing it back as separate steps.
Assuming a bug is fixed because it did not happen in ten tries.

blocks.text: Make shared updates atomic, for example UPDATE scores SET points = points + 1, or use locks.
Describing a bug step by step, even to a rubber duck, forces you to check assumptions you skipped in your head.

steps: Say what you expected to happen
Say what actually happens
Walk through the code line by line, out loud
Notice the step you can’t explain
Check that step first

items: Asking for help with “it doesn’t work” and no steps or error.
Skipping the parts you are sure about, which is where the bug often is.

blocks.text: If you can’t explain a step, that step is where to look.

lessons.title: Writing a test for the bug

blocks.text: A fixed bug can come back with the next change. A test that fails while the bug exists and passes after the fix keeps it from returning unnoticed.

items: Writing the test after the fix without checking that it fails without it.
Testing the implementation details instead of the behavior the user saw.

blocks.text: Reproduce the bug in a test first. Then fix it and keep the test.

title: System Design
description: How to build systems that stay fast and reliable as they grow.

blocks.text: Some answers are expensive to compute but rarely change. A cache keeps a copy of the answer close by, so the next request does not have to do the work again.

steps: A request arrives
Look in the cache
Hit: return the stored answer
Miss: ask the database
Save the answer in the cache for next time

rows: One query until the lesson changes

items: Caching data that must always be current, such as a live duel score.
Forgetting to clear the cache when the data changes.
Giving every entry the same expiry, so they all expire at once and hit the database together.

blocks.text: A cache trades freshness for speed. Decide how out of date each piece of data is allowed to be.
When one server is not enough, there are two ways to grow: make the server bigger, or add more servers.

rows: One machine can only get so big
More machines behind a load balancer
Any server must be able to handle any request

blocks.code:
┌─→ server 1
client → load balancer ├─→ server 2
                      └─→ server 3

items: Keeping sessions in server memory, so a user is logged out when the next request lands on another server.
Adding app servers while the database stays the bottleneck.

blocks.text: Horizontal scaling works when servers keep no state of their own. Put shared state in a database or cache instead.
A load balancer sits in front of several servers and decides which one handles each request. It spreads the work and stops sending traffic to servers that are down.

rows: The server with the fewest open requests
The same server for the same user
A server keeps a local cache per user

items: Skipping health checks, so traffic keeps going to a crashed server.
Depending on sticky sessions so much that one busy user overloads one server.

blocks.text: Spread requests with health checks on, and keep servers interchangeable.
Some work does not need to finish before the user gets an answer, such as sending an email. A queue stores the task so a worker can do it later.

steps: The API puts “send welcome email” on the queue
The API answers the user right away
A worker takes the task from the queue
The worker sends the email
If it fails, the task goes back on the queue for a retry

items: Doing slow work inside the request, so the user waits for it.
Workers that can’t handle the same task twice after a retry.

blocks.text: Queue work that can wait. Make workers safe to run the same task more than once.
Replication keeps copies of the database on other servers. Writes go to the primary, and replicas follow it and can serve reads.

blocks.code:
writes → primary ──┬──→ replica 1 ← reads
                   └──→ replica 2 ← reads

blocks.text: Replicas lag a little behind. A user who just saved something may not see it yet if the next read hits a replica.

items: Reading from a replica right after a write and showing stale data.
Calling replicas a backup; a bad delete is copied to them too.

blocks.text: Replicas add read capacity and failover, not backups. Read your own writes from the primary.
When one database is too big for one server, sharding splits the rows across several databases. A shard key decides where each row lives.

items: Picking a key that sends most traffic to one shard, such as the country.
Sharding before simpler steps like indexes, caching or replicas.

blocks.text: Shard last, and choose a key that spreads both data and traffic evenly.
When servers lose contact with each other, a system must choose: refuse some requests to stay correct, or keep answering and risk being out of date.

rows: Some requests fail until servers agree again
Every request is answered, maybe with old data

items: Assuming the network between servers never fails.
Using the same choice for every kind of data in the app.

blocks.text: Decide per piece of data whether being right or being up matters more.
An operation is idempotent when doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. It makes retries safe after a timeout.

blocks.code:
POST /api/payments
Idempotency-Key: 6f1c-8a20

first try:   payment created
retry:       same key → the server returns the first result

items: Retrying a POST without a key and charging the user twice.
Generating a new key on every retry.

blocks.text: Give risky operations a key, and let the server recognize a repeat.
In a system with many parts, something is always failing somewhere. Good design keeps one broken part from taking down the rest.

steps: Calls to the recommendation service start timing out
A circuit breaker counts the failures
After a few, it stops calling the service for a while
The page shows lessons without recommendations
Later it tries again and closes when calls succeed

items: Letting every page wait on an optional service.
Retrying a failing service so hard that it can never recover.

blocks.text: Use timeouts, fail fast and degrade gracefully when an optional part is down.
A monolith is one app deployed as a whole. Microservices split it into small services that are deployed and scaled separately.

rows: Many teams that need to move independently

items: Starting with microservices for a small team and paying the network cost everywhere.
Splitting services that still share one database and must deploy together.

blocks.text: Start with a well-structured monolith. Split out a service when a real need appears.

title: Infrastructure
description: Where code runs and how it gets there.

blocks.text: Work happens on a branch, apart from the main line. When it is ready, it is merged back, and an automated pipeline takes it the rest of the way.

steps: Push a commit to the branch
CI builds the project
CI runs the tests
The change is reviewed and merged
CD deploys main to production

items: Deploying by hand, so every release is a little different.
Skipping tests to ship faster, then spending longer on the bugs.
Letting a branch live for weeks, so the merge turns into a big conflict.

blocks.text: Automate the path from commit to production, so every release goes through the same checks.
The same code runs on your machine, on a test server and in production. What changes between them is configuration, not code.

blocks.code:
config/
├── development    local database, detailed logs
├── staging        test server, data close to the real thing
└── production     real users, secrets loaded from a vault

blocks.text: Secrets such as database passwords and API keys come from the environment when the app starts. They never live in the repository.

items: Committing passwords or API keys to the repository.
Building a different version of the app for each environment.
Testing only on your own machine, where the setup differs from production.

blocks.text: Build once, configure per environment, and keep secrets out of the code.
A container packs an app together with everything it needs to run: the runtime, libraries and settings. It runs the same on a laptop and on a server.

blocks.code:
FROM node:22-alpine      start from a small image with Node
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci               install exact dependencies
COPY . .
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

items: Saving data inside the container, where it is lost when the container is replaced.
Baking secrets into the image.

blocks.text: A container is a repeatable package for running an app. Keep data and secrets outside it.
An image is the built, unchangeable package. A registry stores images, so every environment can pull exactly the same one.

steps: CI builds the image once
It is tagged with the commit, e.g. devbrawl-api:4f2a9c
CI pushes it to the registry
Staging pulls and runs that tag
Production later pulls the very same tag

items: Deploying the tag latest, so nobody knows which version is running.
Rebuilding the image for production instead of reusing the tested one.

blocks.text: Build once, tag by commit, and promote the same image from staging to production.
With many containers on many machines, someone has to start them, restart them and spread them out. An orchestrator such as Kubernetes does that job.

rows: Starts 3 and replaces any that crash
Places them on machines with room
Replaces copies one by one with no downtime

items: Reaching for an orchestrator for one small app on one server.
Not setting health checks, so it can’t tell a stuck container from a healthy one.

blocks.text: You describe the state you want; the orchestrator keeps the system in that state.
Servers, databases and networks can be described in files instead of clicked together by hand. The files are reviewed and versioned like any other code.

items: Fixing production by hand, so it drifts from what the files describe.
Applying changes without reviewing the plan of what will change.

blocks.text: Describe infrastructure in code, review it, and change it only through the code.
Monitoring answers “is it working right now?” before users have to tell you. A few well-chosen numbers say a lot about a service’s health.

rows: How close is it to its limits?

items: Alerting on everything, so real alerts get ignored.
Measuring averages only, which hide the slow requests users feel.

blocks.text: Watch rate, errors, latency and saturation, and alert only on what needs a person.
People type names like devbrawl.io; computers connect to addresses like 203.0.113.7. DNS translates one into the other.

steps: The browser asks a resolver for devbrawl.io
The resolver asks who handles .io
Then it asks who handles devbrawl.io
That server answers with the address
The answer is cached for its TTL

items: Changing a DNS record and expecting everyone to see it instantly despite a long TTL.
Forgetting to renew the domain.

blocks.text: DNS maps names to addresses, and caches mean changes spread slowly. Lower the TTL before a planned move.
A reverse proxy such as nginx receives every request first and passes it on to the right app. It handles shared jobs so the apps don’t have to.

blocks.code:
devbrawl.io/          → frontend
devbrawl.io/api/      → API
devbrawl.io/hubs/     → API (WebSockets)

the proxy also: terminates HTTPS, compresses, limits body size

items: Forgetting the proxy has its own limits, such as the maximum upload size.
Not forwarding WebSocket upgrades, so live features fail behind the proxy.

blocks.text: The proxy is part of the request path. When something fails between client and app, check it too.
Sometimes a release breaks something despite the tests. The fastest fix is often to go back to the last version that worked, then investigate calmly.

Debugging in production while users keep hitting the bug.

blocks.text: Keep every release easy to undo. Roll back first, then find the cause.
